name: Dong Son culture
title: The story of the Dong Son culture

text: About 3,000 years ago, the Dong Son people farmed rice by the Red River in northern Vietnam.
They kept water buffalo and pigs, and cooked sticky rice in a special pan.
src: c. 1000 BCE: The Đông Sơn culture emerges from the Gò Mun culture in northern Vietnam / The Đông Sơn people were skilled rice farmers / centred on the Red River Delta of northern Vietnam
who kept water buffalo and pigs / a pan for cooking sticky rice

text: They fished and sailed in long dugout canoes, boats made from hollowed-out tree trunks.
src: fished, and sailed in long dugout canoes

text: Their metal workers were skilled at casting bronze, and they made great bronze drums.
One drum weighs 72 kilograms, and making it needed at least a tonne of copper ore, rock that holds the metal.
src: The Đông Sơn people were skilled bronze casters, as the drums found widely through northern Vietnam and in Yunnan and Guangxi show
The Cổ Loa drum weighs 72 kilograms, and casting it would have required the smelting of between 1 and 7 tonnes of copper ore.

text: The drums show a sun, frogs, warships and warriors wearing feather headdresses.
They were beaten in war, at feasts and when people mourned their dead.
src: Heger I bronze kettledrums decorated with a sun, frogs, warships and feather-headdressed warriors
The bronze drums were used in war / in mourning and at feasts

text: A Han Chinese army later conquered the Red River lands, and drum-making came to an end.
Today their drums, first dug up at the village of Dong Son, can be seen in Vietnam's museums.
src: After the Han general Ma Yuan conquered the Red River Plain, the bronze drum culture disappeared.
from the village of Đông Sơn in Thanh Hóa province, where bronze drums were first excavated in 1924 / Displays of Đông Sơn drum surfaces can be seen in several of Vietnam’s cultural institutions.
